content: 1. Administer 5 g of ampicillin orally in combination with 1 g of probenecid. For patients weighing less than 20 kg: Administer 50 mg/kg/day orally, divided into doses every 6–8 hours. For patients weighing more than 20 kg: Administer 250 mg orally every 6 hours. 2. For intravenous (IV) or intramuscular (IM) administration: For patients weighing less than 40 kg: Administer 25–50 mg/kg/day, divided into doses every 6–8 hours. For patients weighing more than 40 kg: Administer 250–500 mg IV/IM every 6 hours. 3. For severe infections requiring higher doses: Administer 150–200 mg/kg/day IV/IM, divided into doses every 3–4 hours. Begin with IV infusion therapy and transition to IM injections if preferred. 4. For infants under 3 months of age: The safety and efficacy of ampicillin have not been established. For infants older than 3 months: Administer oral dosages on an empty stomach. 5. Ampicillin reduces the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine, due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live bacterial vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic therapy is completed. 6. Ampicillin interacts with the cholera vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid coadministration of systemic antibiotics with the cholera vaccine, as these agents may inactivate the vaccine strain. Do not administer the cholera vaccine to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 7. Tetracyclines, such as doxycycline, eravacycline, minocycline, omadacycline, oxytetracycline, sarecycline, and tetracycline itself, may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins, including ampicillin. Monitor for reduced therapeutic effects of penicillins when used concomitantly with tetracyclines. Avoid or consider alternative drugs if necessary. 8. Ampicillin decreases the efficacy of oral microbiota products due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. 9. Ampicillin increases the levels of methotrexate by reducing renal clearance. Use caution and monitor closely for increased serum methotrexate concentrations, which may lead to hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicity. 10. Ampicillin decreases the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, camrelizumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab, through unspecified mechanisms. Use caution and monitor closely, as coadministration may interfere with the therapeutic effects of these agents. 11. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), such as esomeprazole, lansoprazole, omeprazole, pantoprazole, and rabeprazole, reduce the levels or effects of ampicillin by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 12. Ampicillin decreases the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives, such as ethinyl estradiol, levonorgestrel, dienogest/estradiol valerate, and mestranol, by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of these hormones. There is a low risk of contraceptive failure, but additional or alternative forms of birth control may be advisable during concomitant use. 13. Ampicillin decreases the levels of atenolol by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 14. Ampicillin interacts with aspirin (oral and rectal forms) and aspirin/citric acid/sodium bicarbonate by competing for plasma protein binding, which may increase the levels of either drug. Use caution and monitor closely. 15. Ampicillin decreases the levels of rifampin by increasing its metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 16. Ampicillin increases the levels of spironolactone through an unspecified mechanism, potentially leading to hyperkalemia. Use caution and monitor potassium levels closely. 17. Ampicillin interacts with allopurinol, leading to an increased incidence of rash. The mechanism is unknown, and the clinical significance is unclear. 18. Ampicillin decreases the levels of atenolol by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 19. Ampicillin decreases the levels of chloramphenicol, clarithromycin, erythromycin (various forms), and roxithromycin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. 20. Ampicillin interacts with thiazide diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide, chlorothiazide, methyclothiazide, and metolazone, by decreasing renal clearance, which may increase ampicillin levels. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown.
